prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and timely problem: open-vocabulary EEG-to-text decoding from non-invasive recordings, with the central idea of improving downstream decoding by pretraining a joint EEG-text model. The proposed approach combines a contrastive EEG-text objective with masked autoencoding over both modalities, and then transfers the learned EEG-side representations into a BART-based decoder. The topic is compelling, the motivation is reasonable, and the paper is clearly aiming at a meaningful gap in the literature: most prior EEG-language work either focuses on EEG-only pretraining or directly fine-tunes a language model without a dedicated multimodal pretraining stage. The proposed CET-MAE and E2T-PTR framework are therefore directionally interesting, and the empirical gains over several baselines on ZuCo suggest that the approach has promise.

At a high level, I find the paper’s main strength to be its attempt to unify cross-modal alignment and within-modal reconstruction in a single pretraining framework tailored to EEG-text pairs. This is a sensible design choice. Contrastive learning alone can encourage coarse semantic alignment while ignoring modality-specific structure; masked modeling alone can overemphasize reconstruction without sufficiently enforcing pairwise matching. The paper’s framing of these objectives as complementary is convincing and consistent with trends in multimodal SSL. The addition of sentence-level EEG features to compensate for missing word-level fixations is also practically motivated by the peculiarities of ZuCo, and the transfer setup into a generative BART decoder is a natural downstream use case.

The experimental section is reasonably extensive in breadth. The authors report results on three-, four-, and five-task combinations of ZuCo, compare against several prior methods, include ablations on sentence-level EEG and pretraining components, and compare CET-MAE against reduced SSL variants (contrastive-only and masked-only). These are all useful ingredients in a paper of this kind. The qualitative examples also help illustrate what the model is and is not capturing, especially the recurring difficulty with named entities.

That said, I have substantial concerns about the rigor of the empirical claims, the clarity of the setup, and the fairness and interpretability of the comparisons. These concerns are serious enough that, in its current form, I would find it difficult to fully trust the claimed state-of-the-art improvements.

The first major issue is evaluation protocol clarity and possible leakage or overreliance on text-side supervision. The paper states in the limitations that the results “still depend on the implicit use of teacher forcing,” and earlier says that during testing the model operates with an “implicit understanding” of the ground-truth tokens. This is a very concerning formulation. For a decoding task, the exact inference protocol must be unambiguous: what inputs are available at test time, whether generation is fully autoregressive, whether any gold prefix tokens are supplied, whether decoding is conditioned only on EEG embeddings, and whether beam search is used. If teacher forcing or gold-token conditioning is used during evaluation, then BLEU/ROUGE numbers are not directly comparable to standard free-generation settings and may substantially overestimate practical decoding performance. This point is especially important because the paper’s headline claim is improved EEG-to-text decoding. The current wording leaves too much ambiguity about whether the task is true generation from EEG alone or a partially conditioned reconstruction task.

Relatedly, the role of BART is not sufficiently disentangled from the role of EEG. Since BART is a powerful pretrained language model, improvements in BLEU/ROUGE may partly reflect stronger language priors rather than better EEG grounding. The paper would be much stronger if it included analyses that quantify how much information is actually coming from EEG. For example, one would want controls such as decoding from shuffled EEG-text pairs, decoding from sentence length or trivial metadata, or replacing EEG with noise while keeping the same BART decoder. Without such controls, it is hard to assess whether the model is genuinely decoding semantic content from EEG or mostly leveraging the language model to reconstruct plausible sentences from weak cues.

A second major issue is the fairness and consistency of the baseline comparisons. Table 1 mixes results across different sample counts and even different postprocessing conventions regarding repeated words. Some methods are reported from prior work, some are reproduced, and some include parenthetical scores under a different evaluation convention. This makes the comparison difficult to interpret. In particular, the paper emphasizes percentage improvements such as “32.21%” on BLEU-4, but the absolute gain from 6.8 to 8.99 is modest and may or may not be statistically meaningful given dataset size and variance. No confidence intervals, standard deviations across seeds, or significance tests are reported. For a benchmark as small and noisy as ZuCo, reporting single-run numbers is not sufficient to support strong SOTA claims. This is especially true when many gains in the ablations and SSL comparisons are on the order of 0.2–0.5 BLEU.

The third issue is that the paper’s methodological description is incomplete in several places, making reproducibility difficult. Important missing details include the exact EEG feature representation used as input tokens, dimensionalities before and after projection, whether subjects are mixed or split, whether evaluation is subject-dependent or cross-subject, how sentence-level EEG features are computed, how missing word-level fixations are represented, how the contrastive loss is implemented (temperature, in-batch negatives, symmetric or asymmetric objective), and how BART is connected to the transferred EEG representations during fine-tuning. The paper says the BART encoder is frozen in CET-MAE pretraining but later says BART is fully fine-tuned in E2T-PTR; however, the exact interface between EEG embeddings and BART’s encoder-decoder stack is not clearly specified. Is EEG fed as encoder hidden states? Are there cross-attention layers? Is the text encoder reused at all in downstream training? These are central architectural details, not minor omissions.

The fourth issue concerns the novelty claim. The paper presents CET-MAE as the first pretrained EEG-text model for EEG-based language decoding. This may be directionally true depending on how narrowly “pretrained EEG-text model” is defined, but the paper should be more careful. Prior work such as EEG2Text, BELT, UniCoRN, and related cognitive-signal/language alignment methods already explore various forms of EEG-language supervision, alignment, and transfer. The specific combination of contrastive learning plus masked autoencoding in a multi-stream architecture may be novel in this domain, but the broader claim should be softened and situated more precisely relative to existing multimodal EEG-language models.

I also have concerns about the interpretation of the sentence-level EEG token. The paper argues that concatenating sentence-level EEG as an additional token alleviates incoherent semantics caused by missing word-level fixations. This is plausible, and the ablation suggests it helps. However, it also changes the task substantially by injecting a global sentence representation that may carry strong information about the target text. If the sentence-level EEG is recorded over the entire reading of the sentence, then using it to decode the same sentence is reasonable, but it should be discussed more explicitly as a form of global target-side signal. The paper should clarify whether this makes comparisons to methods using only word-level EEG fully fair. More importantly, it would be useful to report results separately for word-only, sentence-only, and combined inputs, and perhaps analyze performance as a function of natural masking ratio or fixation sparsity.

The masking strategy itself is interesting but under-justified. The paper claims that 75% masking on both EEG and text works best, and explains this partly by natural masking already present in EEG due to missing fixations. However, the empirical support is limited to a small grid in Table 3, and the best BLEU-1 actually occurs at 25/25 while higher-order BLEU favors 75/75. This suggests the effect is nuanced. Also, the formula for “overall masking ratio” combines natural missingness and artificial masking, but it is not obvious that these are equivalent from the model’s perspective. Natural missingness is structured and correlated with reading behavior, whereas random masking is synthetic. The paper should be more cautious in interpreting these as additive.

Another weakness is that the qualitative examples, while helpful, also reveal how far the task remains from robust semantic decoding. Many outputs appear to preserve local syntax and common phrases while failing on named entities and content words. This is not a criticism of the authors per se, since the task is genuinely hard, but it does suggest that BLEU/ROUGE may not fully capture whether the model is decoding meaningfully from EEG. Additional analyses such as entity accuracy, content-word F1, semantic similarity metrics, or human evaluation would strengthen the paper. In particular, because BART can generate fluent text, lexical overlap metrics may overstate progress if the model mostly reconstructs common templates.

The ethics statement is too brief. The claim that the authors “do not anticipate any harmful applications” is not persuasive for brain decoding work. Even though the current system is far from practical mind reading, research on neural decoding raises clear privacy, consent, and misuse concerns. A stronger ethics discussion should acknowledge these issues, explain why the present setup is limited to text-evoked reading EEG under controlled conditions, and discuss safeguards and realistic boundaries of applicability.

There are also several presentation issues. The writing is understandable overall but often awkward and repetitive, with many grammatical errors and overstatements. Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially around “significant advancements” and “more powerful and widespread BCI applications.” The tables are somewhat hard to parse, and the notation is occasionally inconsistent. The paper would benefit from careful editing for clarity and precision.

Despite these concerns, I do think there is a real contribution here. The combination of multimodal SSL objectives for EEG-text pretraining is a worthwhile idea, and the empirical results suggest that such pretraining can help downstream EEG-to-text generation. The ablation comparing CET, ET-MAE, and CET-MAE is particularly useful, even if the gains are small. The paper could become much stronger with a more rigorous experimental protocol and clearer exposition.

To improve the paper, I would strongly recommend the following. First, clarify the downstream decoding protocol in exact detail, especially test-time conditioning and whether evaluation uses teacher forcing or gold prefixes. If it does, report fully autoregressive results as the primary metric. Second, add variance estimates across multiple random seeds and statistical significance tests for all main comparisons. Third, include stronger controls to verify EEG grounding, such as shuffled-pair baselines, noise-input baselines, and perhaps ablations that freeze or weaken BART. Fourth, make baseline comparisons strictly apples-to-apples under the same data splits, preprocessing, decoding settings, and repeated-word handling. Fifth, provide more architectural and implementation detail so the method is reproducible. Sixth, add analyses beyond BLEU/ROUGE, especially for named entities and content words, and ideally some semantic or human evaluation. Seventh, moderate the novelty and impact claims and expand the ethics discussion.

My overall assessment is that the paper addresses an important problem and proposes a plausible, potentially useful method, but the current evidence falls short of fully substantiating the strength of the claims. The main blockers are ambiguity in evaluation, insufficiently rigorous comparisons, and limited evidence that the gains reflect improved EEG decoding rather than stronger language-model priors. If these issues are addressed, the work could make a meaningful contribution to EEG-language modeling.

In summary, I view this as a promising paper with interesting ideas and encouraging results, but not yet at the level of rigor expected for a top-tier machine learning venue.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes CET-MAE, a self-supervised pretraining framework for EEG-text representation learning that combines masked reconstruction of EEG/text with EEG-text contrastive alignment via a multi-stream transformer. It then introduces E2T-PTR, which transfers the pretrained EEG-side modules into a BART-based EEG-to-text decoder. Experiments on ZuCo reading-task combinations report modest gains over prior EEG-to-text systems on BLEU and ROUGE, and ablations suggest benefits from combining sentence-level EEG features, pretraining, and the joint SSL objective.
strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: open-vocabulary EEG-to-text decoding from non-invasive signals.
The proposed pretraining objective is intuitively motivated, combining cross-modal contrastive alignment with intra-modal masked reconstruction.
The architecture is reasonably novel for this domain, especially the explicit EEG/text/joint streams and transfer into a downstream decoder.
Includes several ablations: masking ratios, sentence-level EEG inclusion, and comparisons among contrastive-only, MAE-only, and combined SSL variants.
Uses established public datasets (ZuCo 1.0/2.0) and compares against relevant prior work/reproductions.
weaknesses: Empirical gains are generally small in absolute terms for the main controlled comparisons (e.g., improvements over DeWave or reproduced baselines are often under 1 BLEU point and around 1.9 ROUGE-1 F1 at best), while the paper sometimes overstates them as major advances.

Comparisons are not consistently fair across methods because training sample counts differ substantially (10710, 14407, 18791), and some baselines are reproduced while others are taken from prior papers with different evaluation conventions.
The paper lacks statistical significance testing or variance across random seeds, which is especially problematic given the small reported improvements.

Methodological details are insufficient for reproducibility: exact preprocessing, EEG feature construction, tokenization, contrastive loss formulation/temperature, negative sampling, and decoding settings are not fully specified in the main paper.

The role of teacher forcing and the statement that testing uses an 'implicit understanding of ground-truth word tokens' raises concern about evaluation protocol clarity and whether the setup reflects realistic decoding.
Qualitative examples reveal substantial failures on named entities and semantic fidelity, suggesting the task remains far from robust decoding despite optimistic claims.
The paper does not compare against simpler alternatives such as direct BART fine-tuning with sentence-level EEG augmentation but without the complex pretraining, beyond limited ablations.
No analysis is provided on cross-subject generalization, subject splits, or whether gains hold uniformly across tasks/subjects, which is crucial in EEG settings.
methodological_flaws: The evaluation protocol is ambiguously described. The statement that during testing the model operates with an 'implicit understanding of the ground-truth word tokens W' is scientifically problematic and suggests possible leakage or at least unclear use of teacher forcing. If decoder inputs depend on gold tokens at inference, the reported generation quality may not reflect true EEG-to-text decoding.

Claims of 'significant' superiority are not supported by statistical evidence. Reported improvements are small and no confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests are provided, undermining empirical validity.

The headline percentage improvements in the abstract (e.g., 32.21% BLEU-4) appear to be relative improvements over a selected baseline rather than absolute gains, which can exaggerate practical impact; this presentation is potentially misleading.

Baseline comparisons mix different dataset sizes and evaluation conventions (e.g., repeated-word handling, reproduced vs reported numbers), weakening causal attribution that CET-MAE/E2T-PTR is responsible for the gains.

The ablation in Table 5 changes multiple factors in sequence and does not isolate all confounders cleanly; for example, adding sentence-level EEG, adding CET-MAE, and adding E2T-PTR are not compared against all relevant simpler controls.

The masking-ratio conclusion is based on limited trial-and-error settings without rigorous hyperparameter search or uncertainty estimates; asserting that 75% 'can achieve the best results' is weakly supported.

The paper argues that sentence-level EEG alleviates missing word-level fixations, but this is not directly validated through targeted analyses correlating natural masking ratio with performance gains.

There is no mathematical depth or proof burden here, but the loss design and multi-stream mechanism are only informally justified; no analysis shows why excluding masked learnable vectors from the text stream avoids biased contrastive learning beyond intuition.
